transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today? Is there something specific that’s been troubling you?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I, um, I actually decided to come in because... well, it’s my work, mostly, that made me realize something isn't right. I’ve been a credit counselor and loan officer for a long time, and I’ve always prided myself on being sharp, you know? Helping people figure out their finances, looking at all those numbers, making sure everything balances—it requires a lot of attention to detail and you really have to be on the ball. 

But lately, I just... I can’t seem to keep my mind on things the way I used to. It's been incredibly frustrating. I’ll be sitting at my desk, and I'll pull up a loan worksheet or, say, my client follow-up list for the afternoon, and I will just stare at it. I mean, I literally reread the same line over and over again, and nothing sinks in. It’s like looking at a foreign language sometimes, even though I’ve done this a million times and I know these forms like the back of my hand. 

And then, because I can't process it, I end up putting off making my calls entirely. I just push them to the side because even figuring out what to say to the client or making simple decisions about a file feels... I don't know, it just feels so much harder than it should be. It’s taking me twice as long to do half the work, and I just keep sitting there, looking at the screen, trying to force my brain to work the way it used to, and it just won't cooperate.
Can you tell me more about these difficulties with concentration and decision-making? Do they happen only at work, or do you notice them in other areas of your life as well?

Outside of work... gosh, you know, I haven't really thought about it like that. Let me think. I mean, my life outside the office is just so incredibly routine at this point. I've got my systems at home, and everything kind of runs on autopilot. When I leave the branch, I usually just go straight home, or maybe I'll stop at the grocery store, but even then, I'm buying the exact same things I've bought for the last ten years. I don't really stand in the aisle debating between two brands of dish soap or trying to compare the price per ounce, I just grab the blue bottle I always get and keep moving. 

So there aren't really any big decisions to make in my personal time, not like when you're trying to figure out if a client's debt-to-income ratio is going to completely disqualify them for a consolidation loan, or if we can find a workaround. That takes real brainpower and focus. At home, I'm just... well, I might put the television on, maybe watch the evening news or some program where it doesn't really require much of me. If my mind wanders during a commercial or I don't catch every word the anchor says, it doesn't really matter, does it? There's no consequence to it. Nobody's financial future is riding on whether I paid attention to a sitcom. 

So I can't honestly say I've noticed it happening with other things, or at least, I'm not sure if it is. It's really just the office where it's glaringly obvious to me, because that's where people are relying on me to be on top of every single detail, and it's just... it's just so apparent there when I'm staring at a spreadsheet for twenty minutes and nothing is computing. But outside of that, I really couldn't say for sure.

Have you ever found yourself in a situation at home or in your personal life—maybe when something unexpected happens or you have to make a new decision—where you struggle to focus or make a choice, similar to what you described at work?

Gosh, unexpected things... well, to be perfectly honest with you, Doctor, I try very, very hard to make sure unexpected things just don't happen in my personal life. I've always been a planner. You kind of have to be in my line of work, you know? When you're dealing with people's credit scores and loan approvals, there's no room for surprises, because a surprise usually means a hidden bankruptcy or an undisclosed debt, and that ruins a whole application. So I carry that cautious mindset over into my home life. 

I have my schedule, I have my routines, like I mentioned with the grocery store. I suppose... hmm, let me think. Was there a time recently? I mean, a few weeks ago my toaster broke, which I suppose is unexpected, right? You go to make your morning English muffin and the lever just snaps. But I didn't really struggle with a decision there. I didn't sit there agonizing over it. I just drove over to the store and bought the exact same brand I've had since, oh, it must have been 2008 or so. I didn't stand in the appliance aisle comparing the two-slice versus the four-slice, or looking at the ones with the fancy digital screens and the special bagel settings. I just grabbed the one that looked like my old one. 

I just don't really put myself in positions where I have to make new, complex choices outside of the office. My sister sometimes tries to get me to change things up, suggesting new restaurants if we meet for a bite, or asking me to help plan what to bring to a family get-together, and I just tell her to pick whatever she wants. I tell her, "Susan, you know I don't care, just tell me what time to be there and what you need me to buy." It's just easier that way, letting someone else decide. 

So, no, I really can't say I've had a moment at home where I'm sitting there paralyzed trying to make a choice, because I just avoid making them entirely if they aren't part of my usual routine. It's just the work stuff that really throws me. Because at the bank, I *have* to make those decisions. I'm paid to make them, and people are waiting on me, and I just can't seem to do it anymore without feeling like I'm wading through molasses. But at home? No, it just doesn't really come up.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things the way you used to, or that you don’t really feel like doing much of anything, even things you used to like?

Well, to be perfectly honest, yes. That’s exactly it, and it’s been bothering me quite a bit. It’s hard to describe, but most days there’s just this... this dull heaviness sitting with me. It’s not like I’m crying all the time or having some big breakdown, it’s just this constant, heavy feeling right in my chest or on my shoulders that follows me from the minute I wake up. 

And it really has bled into the things I used to love. Take my garden, for example. I have always been so proud of my yard. I have these beautiful hydrangeas along the back fence, and a whole row of hostas, and I used to spend hours out there on my weekends. Just getting my hands in the dirt, pruning the dead leaves, making sure the soil was just right—it used to really lift me up, you know? It was my sanctuary away from all the numbers and the stress of the bank. But lately, I’ll go out there with my gardening gloves and my shears, and I just stand there. I look at the flowers and I feel absolutely nothing. I’m just going through the motions of watering them because I know they’ll die if I don't, not because I'm getting any actual joy out of it. 

And it’s the exact same way at the community center. I’ve been going there for years, especially for the Tuesday morning coffee hour before I head into the branch. I used to love catching up with everyone, hearing about their grandchildren, having a slice of whatever cake someone brought in. But now... I still go, because like I told you, I'm a creature of habit and I don't like breaking my routine, but I’m really just sitting in those folding chairs with a smile pasted on my face. Mary will be talking about her daughter's new house, or someone will be going on about the upcoming bake sale, and I'll nod and smile and say, "Oh, how wonderful," but inside, that dull heaviness is just weighing me down the whole time. I'm just pretending, really. I don't feel that spark or that connection to any of it anymore. It's incredibly exhausting trying to keep up appearances and act like I'm engaged when I just feel so flat and weighed down inside. So yes, I definitely am not enjoying much of anything these days, even the things that used to be the highlight of my week.
Have you noticed that you feel tired or have a lack of energy most days, even when you haven’t been doing much physically?

Oh, heavens, yes. That is... well, that's almost the most frustrating part of all of this, to be completely honest with you. It’s just this constant, overwhelming exhaustion, and it doesn't even make sense because, like you said, I'm really not doing anything physically strenuous. I sit at a desk! I look at financial histories! But I will go to bed, and I'm very good about my routine, I always make sure I get a full night's sleep. I'm usually in bed by 10:00 PM on the dot, and my alarm is set for 6:00 AM. But when that alarm goes off, I wake up and I am just so incredibly tired. I wake up tired even after a full night, and it feels like I haven't slept a wink, even though I know I was in bed the whole time. My limbs just feel like they're made of lead before I've even put my slippers on.

And it just doesn't take much of anything to completely wipe me out anymore. I mean, by the time I’ve done just a couple of client calls—and I'm talking about basic, routine calls, just verifying income documents or explaining the terms of a standard consolidation loan, nothing where I'm running around the branch—or if I just step outside for ten minutes and water the tomatoes... my body feels like I’ve put in a whole day already. I'll just stand there holding the garden hose, looking at the tomato plants, and I'll feel like I just worked a twelve-hour shift during the end-of-year audit. 

It’s just this profound lack of energy. I used to be able to work a full day at the bank, come home, cook a proper dinner, tend to the yard, and still have energy to read a book or call my sister, but now? Now, just making two phone calls and holding a watering can makes me feel like I need to go right back to bed. It’s just so draining. It really makes getting through the week feel like I'm trying to walk through wet cement, because my body is just completely spent before the morning is even over.
Have you ever experienced a time before this one where you felt this same kind of heaviness, lack of energy, or loss of enjoyment in life, even if it got better before?

Well, see, the thing about that question is... there really isn't a "before this one" that got better, because it's all just been *this* time. It's just been one long, continuous stretch. This whole thing—the heaviness, the exhaustion, the not caring about the garden or the community center—this has all been going on since my close friend died a little over two years ago. 

Her name was Margaret. We had known each other for, oh, gosh, it must have been thirty years. We met when I first started working as a teller before I moved up to the loan department, and we were just inseparable. We used to do everything together. When she passed away... well, it was a little over two years ago now, right around the end of the summer. And at first, you know, I just thought it was normal grief. Because of course you're going to be sad when you lose someone who's been such a big part of your daily routine for three decades. You expect to feel heavy and tired. I kept telling myself, "You're just mourning, give it time, you'll bounce back." I'd go to work and tell myself it would pass, that I just needed to push through it. 

But the thing is, Doctor, it just never did. The seasons changed, a whole year went by, and then another year went by... we just passed the two-year mark recently, actually. And that dull heaviness in my chest just never lifted. Not even for a day. I kept waiting for that morning where I'd wake up and feel like myself again, where I'd want to go out and check on the hostas and actually enjoy the sunshine, but it just hasn't happened. 

So, no, I haven't had a time before this that got better. It's just been this one, long, exhausting period ever since Margaret passed. Over two years of just... dragging myself through the days. People always say time heals all wounds, and I suppose I expected that to be true, but I just feel like time stopped for me two years ago and I've been stuck under this wet blanket ever since.
Have there ever been times when your mood was unusually elevated or you felt unusually energetic for several days or more, even if it felt good at the time?

Elevated? Oh, goodness, no. I can't even imagine what that would feel like right now. I mean, to be perfectly honest, I’ve always been a fairly steady, grounded person, even before Margaret passed. Working at the bank, you really have to be. You can't exactly be bouncing off the walls or acting overly enthusiastic when you're sitting down with a young couple trying to figure out if they can afford a thirty-year fixed mortgage, you know? You have to be the voice of reason. But as for being unusually energetic for days at a time... no, absolutely not. 

If anything, I think I’d welcome a day or two of unusual energy just so I could finally get the gutters cleaned out, or maybe organize the filing cabinets in my home office. I have these stacks of old tax returns in there, going all the way back to the late nineties, that I've been meaning to put through the shredder for months. But I just look at the machine and think, 'Oh, I can't possibly sit there and feed the paper through one by one.' So, no, there hasn't been any sort of burst of energy or elevated mood. It's just been this flat, heavy, gray feeling the whole time. 

I sometimes see the younger tellers at the branch, the ones fresh out of their associate programs, and they come in on a Monday morning just buzzing about their weekends, talking a mile a minute, moving a hundred miles an hour, and I just sit there at my desk with my morning tea, feeling like I'm watching a movie in a foreign language. I don't know where people get that kind of pep. I certainly haven't had it. Not for a few days, not even for a few hours. There are no highs for me, just this very long, very exhausting low. I really can't stress enough how much of a struggle it is just to maintain my basic, everyday routine, let alone feel anything even close to elevated. So no, definitely nothing like that.

I'll just stand there holding the garden hose, looking at the tomato plants, and I'll feel like I just worked a twelve-hour shift during the end-of-year audit. 

It’s just this profound lack of energy. I used to be able to work a full day at the bank, come home, cook a proper dinner, tend to the yard, and still have energy to read a book or call my sister, but now? Now, just making two phone calls and holding a watering can makes me feel like I need to go right back to bed. It’s just so draining. It really makes getting through the week feel like I'm trying to walk through wet cement, because my body is just completely spent before the morning is even over.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a prior episode of depression that would help distinguish between a first episode (F32.9) and recurrent depression (F33.9).
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a time before this one where you felt this same kind of heaviness, lack of energy, or loss of enjoyment in life, even if it got better before?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since my close friend died a little over two years ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the history and timeline of the depressive symptoms (whether they occurred before). The 'duration' item explains how long the current continuous episode has been going on, which directly addresses the timeline of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, see, the thing about that question is... there really isn't a "before this one" that got better, because it's all just been *this* time. It's just been one long, continuous stretch. This whole thing—the heaviness, the exhaustion, the not caring about the garden or the community center—this has all been going on since my close friend died a little over two years ago. 

Her name was Margaret. We had known each other for, oh, gosh, it must have been thirty years. We met when I first started working as a teller before I moved up to the loan department, and we were just inseparable. We used to do everything together. When she passed away... well, it was a little over two years ago now, right around the end of the summer. And at first, you know, I just thought it was normal grief. Because of course you're going to be sad when you lose someone who's been such a big part of your daily routine for three decades. You expect to feel heavy and tired. I kept telling myself, "You're just mourning, give it time, you'll bounce back." I'd go to work and tell myself it would pass, that I just needed to push through it. 

But the thing is, Doctor, it just never did. The seasons changed, a whole year went by, and then another year went by... we just passed the two-year mark recently, actually. And that dull heaviness in my chest just never lifted. Not even for a day. I kept waiting for that morning where I'd wake up and feel like myself again, where I'd want to go out and check on the hostas and actually enjoy the sunshine, but it just hasn't happened. 

So, no, I haven't had a time before this that got better. It's just been this one, long, exhausting period ever since Margaret passed. Over two years of just... dragging myself through the days. People always say time heals all wounds, and I suppose I expected that to be true, but I just feel like time stopped for me two years ago and I've been stuck under this wet blanket ever since.

inference.note: The patient has described a persistent depressed mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating that have lasted for over two years, beginning after the death of a close friend. This rules out F32._ (major depressive episode, single episode) because the duration and chronicity are more consistent with recurrent or persistent depressive disorder. F33._ codes (recurrent major depressive disorder) are now more appropriate, with F33.1 (recurrent depressive disorder, current mild episode), F33.2 (recurrent depressive disorder, current moderate episode), or F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder, unspecified) being possible based on severity.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any manic or hypomanic episodes, which would differentiate unipolar depression (F33) from bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Have there ever been times when your mood was unusually elevated or you felt unusually energetic for several days or more, even if it felt good at the time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past manic or hypomanic episodes (unusually elevated mood or energy), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Elevated? Oh, goodness, no. I can't even imagine what that would feel like right now. I mean, to be perfectly honest, I’ve always been a fairly steady, grounded person, even before Margaret passed. Working at the bank, you really have to be. You can't exactly be bouncing off the walls or acting overly enthusiastic when you're sitting down with a young couple trying to figure out if they can afford a thirty-year fixed mortgage, you know? You have to be the voice of reason. But as for being unusually energetic for days at a time... no, absolutely not. 

If anything, I think I’d welcome a day or two of unusual energy just so I could finally get the gutters cleaned out, or maybe organize the filing cabinets in my home office. I have these stacks of old tax returns in there, going all the way back to the late nineties, that I've been meaning to put through the shredder for months. But I just look at the machine and think, 'Oh, I can't possibly sit there and feed the paper through one by one.' So, no, there hasn't been any sort of burst of energy or elevated mood. It's just been this flat, heavy, gray feeling the whole time. 

I sometimes see the younger tellers at the branch, the ones fresh out of their associate programs, and they come in on a Monday morning just buzzing about their weekends, talking a mile a minute, moving a hundred miles an hour, and I just sit there at my desk with my morning tea, feeling like I'm watching a movie in a foreign language. I don't know where people get that kind of pep. I certainly haven't had it. Not for a few days, not even for a few hours. There are no highs for me, just this very long, very exhausting low. I really can't stress enough how much of a struggle it is just to maintain my basic, everyday routine, let alone feel anything even close to elevated. So no, definitely nothing like that.

inference.note: The patient has described a persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, significant fatigue, and difficulty concentrating, all of which have been present for over two years following the death of a close friend. There is no history of a prior episode, and the symptoms have not remitted, suggesting a chronic course. The absence of manic or hypomanic symptoms rules out bipolar disorder, and the duration and severity of symptoms point to a diagnosis of Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) rather than Major Depressive Disorder, which typically involves episodes rather than such a prolonged unbroken course.
